analysis.one_liner: Lets state occupational licensing boards escape antitrust suits only if their states loosen licensing rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Mike Lee with 2 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2015 Supreme Court decision (North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC) exposed state licensing boards, which are often run by the practitioners they regulate, to antitrust lawsuits when they act to limit competition. This bill would give those boards back their legal immunity, but only if the state first agrees to rein in licensing: adopt a policy of using the least restrictive rule possible to protect the public, let workers challenge licensing rules in court with the state bearing the burden of proof, and periodically review its licensing rules against other states' approaches. States could satisfy the conditions either by creating a state office that must approve board actions in writing, or by authorizing court challenges with attorney fees for winners. It never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to enter licensed occupations without paying for years of schooling and exams; consumers, who pay higher prices where licensing restricts the number of providers; entrepreneurs trying to launch new business models that incumbents have fought with licensing; and the bill specifically asks states to evaluate recognizing the existing licenses of active-duty military spouses, who must often re-license after each move [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Aspiring workers, consumers, and military spouses

how_it_helps.text: Conditions antitrust immunity for licensing boards on a state policy that licensing be used only against real, substantial threats to public health or safety when less restrictive alternatives (registration, inspections, insurance, certification) will not suffice [S2][S3].

Gives workers and businesses a defense against enforcement of a licensing rule and a cause of action to challenge it, shifting the burden to the state to prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that the rule protects the public and is the least restrictive option — with attorney fees for people who win [S3].

Requires states to review about 20% of their licensed occupations each year so every licensing rule gets reexamined within five years, including comparing rules to other states' and assessing reciprocity compacts and recognition of military spouses' licenses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent license holders and the licensing boards they sit on, who would face easier entry by competitors and lose much of their ability to enforce licensing against outsiders; states, which would have to fund a new supervision office or court procedures and pay attorney fees when challengers win; and, in fields where licensing genuinely protects health and safety, some reduction in the screening that licensees currently provide.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent licensees, licensing boards, and state budgets

drawbacks.text: The immunity trade cuts both ways: a board whose state adopts the reforms becomes immune from antitrust suits while continuing to license at all, locking in the board's gatekeeper role even as its powers are trimmed [S3].

In occupations where licensing does catch real dangers, replacing it with inspections, bonding, or voluntary certification could leave consumers with weaker protection than mandatory licensing, and the bill's clear-and-convincing-evidence standard makes it harder for states to defend even well-founded rules [S3].
The bill overrides state choices about how to structure their own licensing systems and shifts costs to state taxpayers for new offices, litigation, and fee awards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented problem: state licensing has grown to cover a large share of workers, boards are often controlled by the people they regulate, and incumbents have used licensing to keep competitors out. Its remedy is unusually well built — it does not ban licensing, it forces states to justify each rule and consider lighter-touch alternatives, and it funds challengers who win. The honest objections are the immunity it hands back to compliant boards and the risk of weaker screening in fields where licensing matters; on balance the design addresses the objection by making immunity conditional on real restraint rather than rubber-stamp oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the Restoring Board Immunity Act on July 27, 2017, joined by Sens. Ted Cruz and Ben Sasse, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S3][S5].

The bill responds to the Supreme Court's 2015 decision in North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, which held that self-interested licensing boards may face antitrust liability unless the state actively supervises them [S3].
The bill's findings state that licensing has grown partly because private interests sought it to limit competition, raising prices for consumers and blocking workers and entrepreneurs [S3].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent license holders and the industry-run boards they sit on: the state-enforced barriers to entering their fields stayed exactly as they were, and no state was pushed to review or lighten its licensing rules. Workers priced or trained out of licensed occupations got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it; the bill's findings and structure mirror his long-running push to roll back occupational licensing.

against.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two years remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Three Republicans sponsored the bill and no Democrat signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so opposition never took a recorded shape.

industries.note: Boards, typically staffed by the practitioners they regulate, would win immunity from antitrust suits under the bill, but only by accepting a supervision office or court challenges and a policy that favors less restrictive rules over licensing. The trade would entrench their gatekeeper role while trimming the very power they use to limit competition.

Existing licensees benefit when licensing restricts the number of competitors and supports higher prices. The bill makes every licensing rule challengeable, shifts the burden of proof to the state, and awards attorney fees to workers who win, making incumbent-enforced barriers much harder to maintain.

The bill designates private certification as a preferred alternative to licensing, so states steering away from licensure would create demand for voluntary credential programs that let workers signal skill without blocking entry.
